name: LiteTV Channels
description: Lightweight virtual TV channels: deterministic schedules over your own library, tuned in via normal direct playback at the live position. No transcoding, no tuner emulation.
overview: TV channels from your library, without transcoding.

versions.changelog:
The plugin serves the app's updates. The television has been getting its builds over ADB, which is the only reason ADB is switched on at all - a standing way into the box kept open so an APK can be pushed. The app already knows how to update itself from a URL, so the plugin is now the thing at the other end of it: upload a build on the configuration page, and the television is offered it the next time it looks. Put the address the page shows into the app's Settings -> Advanced -> Update URL once, and that is the last time anything has to be installed by hand.

It answers in the shape the app expects, exactly. The version is written the way the app's own parser reads it, and the assets are advertised under the names it asks for, in the order it asks - which is the whole contract, and every part of it fails silently: an update that is simply never offered, with nothing in any log to say why. Each ABI gets its own name, a release build is never offered under a debug name, and downloads support range requests so a television that loses the connection half way can carry on.

LiteTV is in the dashboard menu, and out of everyone else's sidebar. The link it used to add through Plugin Pages sat in every user's sidebar, not only an administrator's, and what it opened was this page - every channel, every source and the name of the playback account, to somebody who cannot save any of it. The page belongs in the dashboard, which is administrators only, and it is now in the dashboard's own menu beside the other plugins. Any entry left in Plugin Pages by an earlier version is removed on start.

1080p trailers, and the two rules that make them play. The revert to 360p in 1.0.37.0 was one measurement short: adaptive streams do play, they simply come with conditions the plugin was breaking.

Read them in windows. A request for the whole file, or for tens of megabytes, is answered 403; a megabyte at any offset is served happily. ExoPlayer asks for the whole file, which is why the good renditions never showed a frame while 360p muxed ones were fine.

Use them soon. The expire on a googlevideo URL is hours away and means nothing - an address a few minutes old starts refusing everything past its first window. This cached resolutions for forty-five minutes, so a looping channel came back to a break and played a dead URL. It is two minutes now, only enough to stop a break asking twice while it starts; resolving costs a fifth of a second.

Measured: windows of a megabyte at every offset tried, on a URL still answering after five minutes, at 1080p H.264 with 128 kbps AAC. The client has to do the windowing - a player handed these addresses without it will still see 403s.

Trailers use muxed streams again, and play. Pairing adaptive video and audio was right about where the quality lives and wrong about being able to fetch it: measured on 21 August, an adaptive URL serves its first megabyte and answers 403 to everything after it - from any offset, on a URL seconds old, through ANDROID and IOS alike, with or without ratebypass, by Range header or by range query - while a muxed URL from the same answer serves its whole ten megabytes in one request. That is YouTube's proof-of-origin regime, and getting past it means minting a token by running their JavaScript.

So the resolver takes the best muxed format again: itag 18 at 360p for most videos, itag 22 at 720p where it survives. A trailer that plays is worth more than a resolution it never reached. The measurement is written into the code, along with the instruction not to prefer adaptive formats again without first checking that a window past the first megabyte still comes back 206.

The crop tool works on the automatic picture. It used to refuse any slot that had nothing chosen for it, which is the wrong way round: the automatic picture is the one most in need of cropping - nobody chose it for that shape, the plugin found it in the channel's lineup - and the only way to move the frame on it was to upload a copy of a picture the server already had. Cropping one now works exactly as cropping a chosen picture does, and turns it into a chosen picture, which is what saving a crop means anyway. It is fetched at full size rather than at the size of the thumbnail beside the slot, so a crop is a crop of the picture and not of a preview of it.

SponsorBlock, for trailers. German trailers mostly come from channels that wrap them in a branded card at the front and a plea to subscribe at the back, and a minute-long break has no room for either. GET /LiteTv/Trailer/{id} now carries the stretches to seek past, and a client is expected to take them without asking - the skip button an app shows for library content is right for a programme and wrong inside an advert. The lookup uses the hash-prefix form of the API, so the service is asked about every video whose id starts with the same four characters and is never told which one is playing. There is a switch for it on the configuration page; turned off, no request is made at all.

A collection is followed to the films inside it when artwork is derived. A BoxSet is a name with a list behind it and usually has no pictures of its own, so a marathon channel built from one came out blank on the television and offered nothing in the configuration's gallery, while each film it airs has a poster and a thumb. The collection is still asked first: artwork somebody made for a collection was made for exactly this. The web gallery does the same, falling back to the films when the providers hold nothing for the collection itself.

No hardcoded API keys. The trailer resolver carried five AIzaSy keys copied from YouTube's own players, as every port of this trick does. Measured today, the player endpoint answers identically without one - same status, same formats, same 1080p - so they are gone. They look like credentials in a public repository, they belong to somebody else, and they are exactly the sort of constant that gets rotated without notice. What identifies the caller is the client name, its version and a matching User-Agent.

The client ladder is re-measured. ANDROID_VR and the TV player answer LOGIN_REQUIRED, WEB and MWEB answer UNPLAYABLE, IOS answers up to 720p and ANDROID answers the full ladder, so ANDROID leads and IOS backs it up. The failing ones stay behind them, because which of them works is the thing that changes.

The H.264 preference knows its place. It was worth four thousand points against a height in the hundreds, so 360p H.264 beat 1080p VP9 every time; it is a hundred points now, enough to decide between two streams of the same size and never enough to overrule a real difference in resolution. AV1 is skipped, being the codec a set-top box of unknown vintage most often cannot decode in hardware.

Trailers play at the quality the trailer was made at. The resolver took the best of YouTube's muxed formats list whenever a client answered without a manifest, and that list holds itag 18 and little else: 360p with thin audio, which is what the channel was airing. Measured today, no client returns a manifest at all, so the muxed list was always the answer. Everything worth watching lives in adaptiveFormats as separate video and audio streams; the plugin now pairs them - H.264 in MP4 up to 1080p, AAC preferring stereo - and sends both addresses so the client can play them together. Three trailers measured at 1080p, 720p and 800p with 128 kbps audio, in a tenth of a second, where all three were 360p before.

German comes first. A trailer's language now outranks which kind of trailer it is: a household being told about tonight's film in English is worse off than one told about it by a teaser. The markers are the ones the providers actually wrote - Deutsch, German, Offizieller, Kinotrailer - and fourteen of the fifteen films here that have trailers now air a German one. The artwork gallery orders provider pictures the same way: German first, then the ones with no language at all, which is what a textless backdrop is and exactly what the background slot wants.

The crop tool can zoom out. It started at cover and could only ever go further in, so a whole title could never fit inside a banner frame - there is no zoom at which it does, because the whole picture inside the frame leaves bars. The slider now runs down to contain, "Fit whole picture" goes straight there, and the space around the picture is filled with a blurred, over-sized copy of the picture itself rather than black.

The sidebar page shows up. It was registered correctly and served correctly, and it was invisible: the configuration page is a whole document whose outermost element carries Jellyfin's own `page` class, which the web client's CSS hides until its view manager decides to show it - and nothing ever would, because the markup is appended into a container by hand. GET /LiteTv/Page now hands back the body as a fragment with that class removed.

An episode's trailer comes from its series. The metadata providers attach trailers to the series and never to the episode, so a channel advertising "SpongeBob at 20:15" found nothing to play for every break it scheduled. The series' trailer is the right answer anyway: what is being advertised is the programme, and nobody cuts a trailer per episode.

A channel's pictures are the channel's, and they hold still. They were read off the schedule, so a channel's face changed every time its programme did - which is not a face at all, and it changed while somebody was looking at the list. They now come from the channel's own sources and change only when the channel is edited.

Cropping is done by hand, in the configuration page, and once. A banner is about five and a half to one and almost nothing else is, so every picture that is not already a banner lost most of its height to become one - from the middle, with no idea where the faces or the lettering were. Drag to move the frame, zoom, and the cropped picture is uploaded as the slot's own file.

A channel has three pictures now, not one wide one used twice. A banner is made to be looked at with a name over it, which is what a channel card is; a backdrop is the only artwork drawn to fill a screen; a cover is the upright one. Answering the first two with the same file made the channel screen a blown-up version of the card that led to it.

The channel's automatic cover asks the series before the episode. An episode's Primary image is a 16:9 still of one scene - neither upright nor a picture of the channel - which is what turned up in the cover slot.

The configuration page shows what a channel will actually air: times, titles and breaks, day by day. Everything else on that page describes a channel and none of it says what comes out, and a loop of three series on a fifteen-minute grid is not something anybody can hold in their head. A suggested channel now arrives with the same fields a hand-made one has, rather than half of them.

Chosen artwork can be downloaded and kept: POST /LiteTv/Artwork/{channelId}/{kind}/Fetch takes an address and stores the bytes here. A picture from a metadata provider does this automatically, since an address nobody here looks after stops working sooner or later, and a television behind a household firewall may not reach it even while it works. Pictures are drawn whole and in their own shape when choosing, rather than as small wide crops that turn every poster into a slice of somebody's face.

A guide row asks for one wide, specific picture of the programme, and which image that is depends on what the programme is. An episode's Primary image is its still - already the right shape, and the one thing that tells two episodes of a series apart. A film's Primary is its upright poster, and cropping that into a wide row is what left the films looking wrong next to the episodes. Films now ask for the Thumb ("Miniaturansicht"), which is the same artwork drawn wide.

An episode with no still of its own no longer falls through to the series poster, which is the same wrong shape one rung further away; it takes the series' Thumb or backdrop instead. Primary is still the last resort everywhere, because it is the one image nearly everything has and a badly-shaped picture of the right programme beats an empty rectangle.

The channel schedule is edited as a week rather than as three text boxes. Seven tracks, one per day, with every block drawn where it actually sits: drag a bar to move it, drag its right edge to lengthen it, click an empty stretch to start a block there. Trailer slots show as thin marks. The old form is still there and still edits everything - the two are looking at the same objects - but the question nobody could answer before, "what is this channel doing at eight on a Tuesday, and does it collide with anything", is now answered by the picture.

The artwork editor shows what each slot is currently drawn with, including the picture the plugin falls back to when nothing is set - faded and labelled, so a picture that was chosen never looks like one that was found. Artwork can now come from any title in the library, not only the ones the channel airs, and from the metadata providers: TheMovieDB, TheTVDB and Fanart already hold artwork for every item, and asking them is one request.

LiteTV adds itself to the web client's sidebar when the Plugin Pages plugin is installed, so configuring a channel is one navigation rather than three. The page is served at GET /LiteTv/Page and loads itself when nothing fires a dashboard event at it. A server without Plugin Pages gets no link and no stray file.

Channels have artwork of their own. A channel built from one series wears what is on air perfectly well; a channel built from a genre does not - what is on changes every hour, much of it has no wide picture, and during a break there is nothing on air to borrow from at all, which is how a channel card ends up a black rectangle. Each channel can now be given a card picture, a background and a cover, chosen from its own content, pasted as an address, or uploaded. A channel that sets none of them falls back to the first thing in its own lineup that has a picture, so no channel is faceless any more.

The guide can be asked for the breaks as well: GET /LiteTv/Channels/{id}/Now?breaks=true lists interstitials alongside programmes, each naming the programme it advertises. Without it there is no way to see, from the sofa, that trailer scheduling works at all. The upcoming list now goes to 64 entries rather than 20.

New: POST and GET /LiteTv/Artwork/{channelId}/{kind} store and serve an uploaded channel picture. The GET is open, like Jellyfin's own item images, because television clients draw these through an image loader that carries no credentials.

Breaks now advertise a programme a few slots further on rather than the one that starts when the break ends - television says "at eight, the film" an hour beforehand, and a trailer butted against its own programme tells the viewer nothing. How far ahead is the channel's Trailer lookahead, which had been in the configuration all along and was never read. The guide names the programme a break is advertising outright, so a client no longer has to guess it from what follows.

Channels can place trailers themselves: a trailer slot is a standing instruction - this thing, at this time, on these days - claiming the break its start time falls inside. It can name a library item or an address.

Linked trailers, which is nearly all of them, can be resolved into something a television can actually play: GET /LiteTv/Trailer/{itemId} answers with a stream URL and the headers to fetch it with. Trailers are ranked official first, teaser last.

A break is no longer reported as "off air", which made the channel list announce dead air every time a gap came round. The playback account is now forbidden from transcoding, so a channel that cannot direct play fails where it can be seen rather than quietly putting the server to work.

The channels are no longer published to Jellyfin at all - no "TV-Sender" library entry, nothing in Live TV. Both routes gave clients something they could not really play: a channel item is stored once and never re-resolved, so its entries went stale at every changeover, and Live TV hands a client a stream rather than a position in one. The schedule is served as data instead, and a client that understands a channel builds the queue itself. Everything else sees nothing, which is the point.

Channel viewing is now kept off your account by playing it under a Jellyfin account of the plugin's own, created on first use and hidden from the login screen. The server records a playback against whoever the token belongs to, so the viewing lands there however playback started - which the old watch-state shield could never guarantee, because a player that re-prepares itself after a library scan reports playback nobody asked for.

Breaking: the injected web UI is gone, and with it the home row, the guide button and the playback overlays. The Tuned, PlayOn and Playing endpoints are gone too. Clients now ask GET /LiteTv/PlaybackUser for the account to play under, and must refuse to play without it.
